name: Scalp reduction
lead: Scalp reduction is a surgical procedure that makes bald or thinning areas of the scalp smaller by cutting out a section of hairless skin and pulling the neighbouring hair-bearing scalp together. People use it to look as if they have a fuller head of hair: the bald patch is shorter, so the same donor hair covers more of the head, and the remaining hair lies closer together [1][7][8].

The procedure is described in the dermatology and plastic surgery literature from at least 1980, mostly as an adjunct to hair transplantation, and later versions include serial reductions, scalp extension and tissue expansion [1][2][3][9]. Wikipedia describes it as widely practised from the 1960s and rarely performed now, with hair transplantation having taken its place for many patients [10].
Published work consists of technique descriptions, reviews and case reports; no controlled trials comparing outcomes were found [1][2][3][5].

angle.text: People with a bald crown or vertex have used scalp reduction to shrink the area that needs covering, either on its own or ahead of hair transplantation. A related operation, hairline lowering, adapts the same principles to bring a high hairline down [7][8].

paras: The procedure removes bald scalp and advances neighbouring hair-bearing skin to close the gap. A 1980 article reviewed the literature and presented an improved technique for using it alongside transplantation [1]. Later papers addressed repeating the procedure in stages [2] and extending the stretch capacity of the scalp [3].

A 1992 review in Clinics in Dermatology and a 1982 review in Clinics in Plastic Surgery cover the operation under the heading of scalp reduction [11][12]. A 1982 office-surgery review lists scalp reduction alongside hair transplants and scalp flaps as surgical options for male-pattern alopecia [13]. Wikipedia states that suitable candidates have genetic hair loss, an elastic scalp and donor hair at the sides and back, and that a session takes about two to three hours [10].

Serial reductions repeat the excision in stages so the scalp can stretch between operations; a biomechanical analysis of this approach was published in 1999 [2]. Scalp extension uses a thin bioplastic sheet attached with hooks to the galea after reduction, to increase hair-bearing surface; its 1993 description compared outcomes with patients treated by earlier methods [3].

Tissue expansion places a device under the hair-bearing scalp to grow extra skin, and is described alongside older reduction methods for repairing large scalp defects such as scarred areas where transplanted hair is not suitable [14]. A 2013 review notes that hairline lowering, or forehead reduction, was adapted from scalp reduction and flap techniques and is described as best suited to people with a lifelong high hairline and no progressive hair loss [7]. A separate review on the crown discusses technique selection for obtaining a natural look and apparent density [8].
A device for managing suture tension during skin closure was published in 1992 [4].

Scalp reduction is described in the 1980s dermatology literature as a way to cut down the area to be transplanted [1][13]. A 2021 plastic surgeon's review of hair transplant history in India notes that plugs gave way to mini- and micrografts, with scalp reduction playing an important role along the way [16]. Wikipedia describes the operation as very popular from the 1960s and reduced in use as hair transplantation techniques improved [10].

A 1984 case report described scalp reduction as treatment for a patient with cutis verticis gyrata, a condition of folded scalp skin [5]. Reductions and expanders are also used for repairing scalp defects [14].

Wikipedia lists swelling, bleeding around stretched flaps, numbness, rare infection, temporary hair loss, reduced scalp blood flow, scalp thinning and rare scarring as possible complications [10]. Published technique papers focus on closure and tension management, and no complication rates from trials were found [4][2].
No studies found. The literature consists of technique descriptions, reviews and case reports rather than trials with outcome comparisons [1][2][5][14].

timeline.event: A review and improved technique for scalp reduction as an adjunct to hair transplantation is published [1].
Reviews of scalp reduction appear in plastic surgery and dermatology journals [12][13].
Scalp reduction is reported as treatment for cutis verticis gyrata [5].
Scalp extension is described as an alternative to expansion and reduction alone [3].
Serial scalp reductions are analysed from a biomechanical viewpoint [2].
Hairline lowering is reviewed as a procedure adapted from scalp reduction [7].

card.summary: Surgical removal of bald scalp to shrink the bald area; an older hair-restoration adjunct with sparse modern evidence.
card.note: Surgical excision; the literature is mostly older technique papers.

quick.overview:
Scalp reduction cuts out a strip of bald scalp and stitches hair-bearing skin together to shrink the bald area. It has been described in surgical journals since at least 1980, often alongside hair transplants.
The literature consists of technique papers and case reports; no trials exist.
quick.mechanism: Bald skin is excised and neighbouring scalp is advanced and sutured; stretching techniques and serial procedures have been described.
quick.risks: It is a surgical procedure with the usual risks of excision and closure, such as scarring.
